label: After a Breakup
framing: A breakup is a real loss, and Scripture never tells the wounded to pretend otherwise. There is grief here to be felt and not rushed, and a God who is near to the brokenhearted long before you feel near to him.
cultural: Our culture treats a breakup as an embarrassment to recover from quickly, something to be cured by a new match before the bed is cold. It rarely grants that an attachment can be deep and right to mourn even when it was right to end. Scripture honors the wound, refusing both the stoic shrug and the frantic replacement, and gives sorrow its proper hours.
historical: The Psalms gave the church a language for love withdrawn and hope deferred three thousand years before anyone called it heartbreak. Augustine wrote with startling honesty of how a lost love undid him before he learned to rest his heart where it would not be taken away, and generations of believers have found in the laments a place to bring exactly this grief.
application: Let yourself grieve without shame, and resist the rush to numb it with a screen or a rebound. Lean on the friends who knew you before this person, and tell at least one of them the truth about how hard it is. Take stock honestly of what you learned without rewriting the other into a villain or a saint. And let this be a season where your worth is reset on the one love that cannot leave.

verses.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.
verses.where: David's psalm of thanks turns to teaching: the LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. The psalm admits in the next verse that the afflictions of the righteous are many. The site's plain note says that if you are brokenhearted now, this verse is not a sentence to argue with but one to rest on: God is near.

verses.text: And once more she conceived and gave birth to a son and said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” So she named him Judah. Then Leah stopped having children.
verses.where: Leah, married to a man who loved her sister, names her first three sons for her hope that her husband will finally love her. The site's note says the LORD's first act in the chapter is to see the woman Jacob overlooked, and that with her fourth son she stops speaking of her husband and names the boy for praise of the LORD. The plain note speaks to anyone who has felt chosen by no one: God saw Leah when her husband did not, and her sorrow was not the measure of her worth.

verses.text: He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.
verses.where: The hymn praises the LORD who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds, and in the next breath determines the number of the stars and calls each by name. The site's note says each movement of the psalm sets God's power over creation beside his tender care for the lowly. The one who keeps count of the stars is not too great to attend to a broken heart.

verses.text: To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing, a time to search and a time to count as lost, a time to keep and a time to discard, a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace.
verses.where: The Teacher's poem of opposites includes a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing, a time to search and a time to count as lost. The site's note says the poem sets out fourteen pairs of opposites, and that God has made everything beautiful in its time, though people cannot grasp the whole of his work. There is a time to stop searching for what is gone, and it rarely comes as quickly as we would like.

verses.text: For the LORD has called you back, like a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, like the rejected wife of one’s youth,” says your God.
verses.where: God speaks to his exiled people as a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, the rejected wife of one's youth, and says he has called her back. The site's note says the chapter treats the forsaking as brief and the compassion as everlasting. Scripture knows the language of rejection from the inside, and God uses it to speak tenderness.

verses.text: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
verses.where: After twenty verses describing affliction in stark images, the speaker calls to mind the LORD's loving devotion and his mercies, new every morning. The site's note says the chapter lets the pain stand without censoring it, and that the hope in it is chosen rather than felt. Some mornings after a loss, choosing to remember is all a person can do, and it is enough to begin.

verses.text: Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.
verses.where: Paul names two kinds of sorrow: one that leads to repentance and life, and one, sorry mostly for itself, that leads to death. If you were the one who did wrong in the relationship, the way forward is the first kind, honest and fruitful. It is not endless self-punishment, which helps no one, least of all the person you hurt.

verses.text: “Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old. Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert.
verses.where: God tells the exiles not to dwell on the former things, because he is about to do something new, a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert. The site's note says he is announcing a new exodus from Babylon, greater than the first. The word is spoken to people still in exile, not to people told to pretend they were never taken from home.

verses.text: Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
verses.where: Jesus calls everyone who is weary and burdened to come to him and promises rest for their souls. The site's plain note says the invitation is not one more demand but a call from a person, gentle and humble in heart, and that his yoke is made for two. Rest in Christ does not replace other help, the note adds, and getting care when weariness turns into despair is not a lack of faith.

verses.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verses.where: Paul names every power he can think of, death and life, the present and the future, height and depth, and says none of them can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. The site's note says the chapter that began with no condemnation ends with no separation. A human love can end; this one does not.

misread.taken: After a breakup this verse is often offered as a promise that God has someone better planned, that the plans to prosper you mean a new relationship is on its way and the heartbreak will soon make sense.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says the promise was given to the Judean community in exile, that the you is plural throughout, and that it would be fulfilled only after seventy years, so that most adults who first heard it would die in Babylon. The letter was written to answer prophets who promised quick relief. It reveals God's character, his purposes of peace for his people and his faithfulness across generations, and Christians rightly take comfort in that. It is not a guarantee of a problem solved soon or a person sent to replace the one you lost.
misread.text: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.

whole: If someone you used to date is threatening you, following you, or will not leave you alone, your safety comes first: tell someone you trust and get help, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. And if the end of this relationship has brought thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. A breakup is a real loss, and it can take the ground out from under a person. The phone that used to light up now stays dark. Songs, streets and friends all carry the other person's name. Sleep goes, or appetite, and the mind replays every conversation looking for the moment it went wrong. Some are embarrassed by how much it hurts, as if grief were only allowed for a death or a divorce, and some hear from well-meaning Christians that it was not meant to be and that someone better is coming, which can make the pain feel like a failure of faith.

Scripture explains why it hurts so much. God said at the beginning that it is not good for a person to be alone, and a person who has shared their days with someone has given away part of their heart. Rejection reaches past the relationship into the question of worth, as it did for Leah, naming her sons for the love she hoped would come. Some breakups are wisdom, when two people see that a promise would not hold. Some follow wrongs, on one side or both, and some leave a person grieving and guilty at once because they were the one who ended it. And many of us, if we are honest, had begun to ask the other person to be what only God can be: our worth, our future and our rest. That does not make the grief wrong. It explains why it is so heavy.

So the Bible's wisdom is to grieve honestly and slowly. The Psalms give words for it, and there is a time to search and a time to count as lost; that time does not come by being told to move on. Resist the quick cures: another relationship begun to stop the ache, checking the other person's life online, revenge in words or in kind. If you wronged them, the sorrow that leads to repentance looks like an honest apology and changed ways, not endless self-punishment. If they wronged you, forgiveness lets go of revenge over time, and it does not require you to stay in contact. Go back to the friends and the church you may have drifted from, and let them carry some of this with you. In time, ask what you have learned about yourself, without contempt for who you were.

The hope Scripture gives is not that the right person is just around the corner, though some people do love again, and well. It is that the LORD is near to the brokenhearted now, before anything is fixed. God saw Leah when her husband did not, and he called his deserted people back with everlasting compassion. Christ invites the weary to come to him and promises rest. And nothing in all creation, not this loss nor any future one, can separate those who belong to him from the love of God in Christ. Grief does not mean that love failed. It means you loved, and you are still loved.
deep.sit: What have you been asking another person to be for you that only God can be, and what would it look like to let him be that now, while the grief is still real?

prayer.lead: A prayer that hands times and outcomes back to God. Pray it on the nights when the future feels taken.
prayer.text: But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, “You are my God.” My times are in Your hands; deliver me from my enemies and from those who pursue me. Make Your face shine on Your servant; save me by Your loving devotion.

careLines.text: God saw Leah when her husband did not.
Your sorrow is seen too, and it is not the measure of your worth.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
If you are not safe at home, the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
